w: Every periodontal diagnosis starts with the same three numbers. Probing depth (PD) is measured from the gingival margin to the base of the pocket. Gingival recession (GR) is measured from the CEJ to the gingival margin. Clinical attachment level (CAL) — the number that actually matters for staging — is the sum of the two, effectively the distance from the CEJ to the base of the pocket. When the CEJ sits below the margin (no visible recession), GR is recorded as a negative number and CAL comes out smaller than PD; when recession is visible, GR is positive and CAL comes out larger than PD. A 7 mm pocket with the CEJ felt 4 mm subgingival is only 3 mm of attachment loss, while a shallow 2 mm pocket sitting on 4 mm of visible recession is 6 mm of attachment loss — more attachment loss on paper, but a far more maintainable tooth, because the patient can actually reach it with a brush. Radiographs fill in what a probe cannot reach. Periapicals plus vertical bitewings are preferred over horizontal bitewings, because a horizontal film can miss bone loss on one of the two arches entirely. A panoramic gives a useful global view but is not detailed enough to diagnose periodontal disease on its own. Health, gingivitis, or periodontitis Health means no probing depth beyond 3 mm, no bleeding, and no attachment or bone loss. Plaque-induced gingivitis can still show probing depths of 4–5 mm and bleeding on probing, but critically no attachment loss and no bone loss — it is contained entirely within the gingiva and is fully reversible with plaque control. A 10% bleeding-on-probing threshold across the full mouth is used before calling a case gingivitis, since probing pressure varies enough between examiners that two or three isolated bleeding sites should not trigger the diagnosis on their own. Periodontitis is different: attachment loss and bone loss are both present, pockets often reach 6 mm or more, and — unlike gingivitis — the disease is not fully reversible. Treatment can stabilize a periodontitis patient, but the best achievable outcome is health on a reduced periodontium, not a full return to the original attachment level. The periodontium itself can be intact or reduced, independent of disease activity. An intact periodontium can be healthy or have gingivitis. A reduced periodontium — from prior periodontitis, crown lengthening, or simple recession — can also be healthy or inflamed. A previously treated periodontitis patient who is stable on maintenance is diagnosed as healthy on a reduced periodontium, not re-staged, unless disease recurs; if pockets deepen and bleeding returns at a later maintenance visit, the diagnosis shifts back toward periodontitis depending on how widespread the change is. Recession is a sign, not a diagnosis Recession can occur in tissue that has never had periodontitis, so it is classified separately by how much interproximal attachment is also lost. RT1 has no interproximal loss at all and predicts full root coverage. RT2 has some interproximal loss, but buccal recession still exceeds it, predicting partial coverage. RT3 has interproximal loss that exceeds the buccal recession, and root coverage is not attempted because it will not succeed. Staging and grading Staging captures how severe the disease is and how complex it will be to manage, using interdental CAL as the gold standard (radiographic bone loss as a second choice). Stage 1 and 2 track rising CAL and bone loss in the coronal third of the root; Stage 3 and 4 both involve CAL ≥5 mm and bone loss into the middle third or beyond — the two are separated not by more attachment loss, but by tooth loss count (≤4 teeth lost pushes Stage 3, ≥5 pushes Stage 4) and by whether the case needs complex, multidisciplinary rehabilitation. Three findings force a case straight to Stage 3/4 regardless of the CAL math: vertical bone loss ≥3 mm, Class II–III furcation involvement, and any tooth loss attributable to periodontitis. A recurring pitfall: a deep probing depth by itself never proves periodontitis — without confirmed bone loss, a mouthful of 4s and 5s could just be generalized gingivitis. Grading estimates how fast the disease is moving and how the patient is likely to respond. The default assumption is Grade B (moderate), shifted up or down only with evidence. Where serial records exist, direct evidence of progression over time is the gold standard; otherwise, percent bone loss on the worst tooth divided by the patient's age gives a ratio — under 0.25 suggests Grade A, 0.25–1.0 suggests Grade B, and over 1.0 suggests Grade C. Two modifiers can only push the grade up: heavy smoking (more than 10 cigarettes a day) and an HbA1c of 7% or higher both bump a case to Grade C outright, even if the bone-loss/age ratio alone would suggest B. A patient never earns a downgrade simply for not smoking or not having diabetes. Only one stage and one grade are assigned per patient — the stage comes from the single worst site in the mouth, and the grade from progression evidence plus modifiers. Reading a bone defect At flap reflection, a defect is described by how many bony walls remain around the affected root — picture standing inside the defect and counting the walls visible around you. A 3-wall defect (buccal, lingual, and the wall against the neighboring tooth, with only the involved root bare) has the best prognosis for regeneration. A 2-wall defect has lost one of those walls; when bone is gone from both neighboring proximal surfaces and only buccal and lingual walls remain, that specific pattern is called a crater. A 1-wall defect has the worst prognosis. Radiographs can be deceptive here — thick cortical bone, especially on the mandibular buccal/lingual, can mask a defect that only becomes obvious once the flap is raised. From diagnosis to treatment plan Every patient starts with Phase I (non-surgical) therapy, regardless of stage: oral hygiene instruction, scaling and root planing, smoking-cessation counseling, replacement of plaque-retentive restorative margins, and — easy to forget — caries control, restored before or alongside SRP rather than deferred, since a cavitated surface is harder to clean and instrument. Any permanent crown or final RPD waits until periodontal therapy is complete; a temporary crown bridges the gap. The Phase I re-evaluation appointment, not the initial exam, is where the definitive call on surgical (Phase II) therapy gets made, based on how much the tissue improved and how well the patient complied. Stage 1–2 cases often resolve with Phase I alone and move straight to maintenance; Stage 3–4 cases more often need Phase II — resective surgery to recontour bone into a physiologic, cleansable shape, or regenerative surgery to rebuild a favorable defect. Every plan ends in maintenance, and the evidence for it is stark: patients who refuse treatment lose roughly three times as many teeth as treated patients, and even treated patients who skip maintenance lose teeth at about twice the rate of those who keep their recall visits.
